lesson.title: Change the layout without losing the meaning

steps.headline: From a list to a grid

lead.text: The list has one row per record, and the grid has one cell per record. df.pivot(index='shop', columns='month', values='units') builds the grid. The shop values become the row labels, the month values become the column headings, and each units figure moves into the cell where its shop row meets its month column. Nothing is added or changed on the way, so a pivot only rearranges the records.

A cell holds one value, so pivot needs each shop and month pair to appear once. It also matters which way round you ask. The figure pivots four records twice, once with the shops down the side and once with the months.

afterFigure.text: Both grids hold the same four figures. Bay has 2 under Jan and 5 under Feb, and Hill has 3 under Jan and 7 under Feb. In the second grid the figures are the same and the months run down the side. Swapping index and columns turns one into the other. If a pair appeared twice, pivot could not choose between the two figures and would stop with an error, which is what the next screen deals with.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({'shop': ['Bay', 'Bay', 'Hill', 'Hill'], 'month': ['Jan', 'Feb', 'Jan', 'Feb'], 'units': [2, 5, 3, 7]})
result = df.pivot(index='shop', columns='month', values='units')

values.name: result
values.display:
month  Feb  Jan
shop           
Bay      5    2
Hill     7    3

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({'shop': ['Bay', 'Bay', 'Hill', 'Hill'], 'month': ['Jan', 'Feb', 'Jan', 'Feb'], 'units': [2, 5, 3, 7]})
result = df.pivot(index='month', columns='shop', values='units')

values.name: result
values.display:
shop   Bay  Hill
month           
Feb      5     7
Jan      2     3

lead.text: Labels are not cells. A grid holds one measurement for each shop and month combination.

reveal.text: You counted the cells as shops times months. The pivot only rearranges the records into that grid.

lead.text: Real lists are rarely so tidy. Two sales for Bay in January, perhaps from two tills, give two records for the same shop and month. In a grid they have to share one cell, and pivot refuses, because it would have to guess how to combine them.

df.pivot_table combines the records for you once you say how, through its aggfunc argument. With aggfunc='sum' a shared cell holds the total of its records, and with aggfunc='mean' it holds their average.
In the figure, two of the three records are for Bay in January. The grid is built once with each rule.

afterFigure.text: Bay's two January records are 2 and 6. The sum puts 8 in the cell and the mean puts 4. Hill has a single record of 3, which stays 3 either way, because a rule applied to one value returns that value. Neither answer is the true one. Which is right depends on what the records are: tills that each rang up part of a shop's sales should be summed, and repeated readings of one thing might be averaged. State the rule so that the reader knows what each cell contains.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({'shop': ['Bay', 'Bay', 'Hill'], 'month': ['Jan', 'Jan', 'Jan'], 'units': [2, 6, 3]})
result = df.pivot_table(index='shop', columns='month', values='units', aggfunc='sum')

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({'shop': ['Bay', 'Bay', 'Hill'], 'month': ['Jan', 'Jan', 'Jan'], 'units': [2, 6, 3]})
result = df.pivot_table(index='shop', columns='month', values='units', aggfunc='mean')

lead.text: Sometimes you need to go the other way. A grid with one column per month is easy to read but hard to group or plot, which usually want one row per measurement. df.melt reverses a pivot. It takes the month columns and stacks them into two new columns, one for the old column heading and one for the figure that sat under it.

id_vars names the columns that stay attached to every measurement, here the shop. value_vars names the columns to stack. var_name and value_name set the names of the two new columns. The figure melts a small grid twice, first with both month columns and then with only Feb.

afterFigure.text: The first melt turns two shops and two month columns into four rows, one for each shop and month. The second stacks only Feb, so it makes two rows. Every row keeps its shop, so a figure never loses the label that says what it measured. Melting creates no measurements and loses none, because each cell in the stacked columns becomes exactly one row.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({'shop': ['Bay', 'Hill'], 'Jan': [2, 3], 'Feb': [5, 7]})
result = df.melt(id_vars='shop', value_vars=['Jan', 'Feb'], var_name='month', value_name='units')

values.name: result
values.display:
shop month  units
0   Bay   Jan      2
1  Hill   Jan      3
2   Bay   Feb      5
3  Hill   Feb      7

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({'shop': ['Bay', 'Hill'], 'Jan': [2, 3], 'Feb': [5, 7]})
result = df.melt(id_vars='shop', value_vars=['Feb'], var_name='month', value_name='units')

values.name: result
values.display:
shop month  units
0   Bay   Feb      5
1  Hill   Feb      7

lead.text: Every melted row must still say which shop it came from. Something has to tell melt which columns to leave in place.
Each original row gives one long row for every value column that is melted.

reveal.text: Every original row contributed one long row per melted column, so the rows multiplied. No measurement was lost, only moved.

lead.text: A grid has a cell for every shop and month pair, but the list may lack a record for some pairs. Suppose Hill has no record for January. The cell where Hill meets Jan has nothing to show, so pivot_table leaves it missing. That is the same kind of gap you met earlier.

fill_value=0 replaces the missing cells with zero. That is a claim that nothing was sold, and it is true only if a missing record really means none. If the record might simply be absent, a zero gives a false figure. The figure builds a grid from two records, first leaving the empty cells alone and then filling them with 0.

afterFigure.text: With records only for Bay in Jan and Hill in Feb, the grid has four cells and two of them are empty. The first case shows them as missing. The second shows them as 0, and a reader would take those zeros as sales that did not happen. Decide what an empty cell means before you fill it, and say which choice you made.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({'shop': ['Bay', 'Hill'], 'month': ['Jan', 'Feb'], 'units': [2, 7]})
result = df.pivot_table(index='shop', columns='month', values='units', aggfunc='sum')

values.name: result
values.display:
month  Feb  Jan
shop           
Bay    NaN  2.0
Hill   7.0  NaN

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({'shop': ['Bay', 'Hill'], 'month': ['Jan', 'Feb'], 'units': [2, 7]})
result = df.pivot_table(index='shop', columns='month', values='units', aggfunc='sum', fill_value=0)

values.name: result
values.display:
month  Feb  Jan
shop           
Bay      0    2
Hill     7    0

lead.text: A pivot has a cell for every shop and month pair. If no record exists for a pair, that cell is missing.

reveal.text: The cells without records stayed missing. Filling them with zero would have claimed that nothing was sold, which the data did not say.

lesson.orientation: Pivot unique records, aggregate duplicate keys and melt columns back into observations.
lesson.reviewLabel: Change the layout without losing the meaning
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea with a new input.

blocks.text: A shop manager sends a list in which every row is one shop in one month: Bay in each of three months, then Hill in the same three months. With two shops and three months the list has six rows, and each row holds one figure for units sold. A program can filter and group such a list easily, and a person finds it hard to compare.

The person who reads the report wants the other shape: shops down the side, months across the top and one figure in each cell. A row then reads as one shop's months, and a column compares the shops. Moving between the two shapes is called reshaping. It sounds like tidying, and it can go wrong in a way that changes the figures, for instance when two records compete for one cell.
This lesson turns the list into a grid and deals with cells that have two records. It then turns the grid back into a list and looks at what an empty cell means.

intro.promise: By the end you'll turn a long list into a grid and back, and know what to do when two records land in one cell.

recap.keyIdea: pivot arranges records in a grid when each cell has one record, pivot_table combines repeats with a chosen rule, and melt returns the grid to a list.

blocks.text: You counted 6 rows for 2 shops and 3 months. You found 12 cells in a 3 by 4 grid, and 2 empty cells where no record existed.

recap.nextHook: You can now clean text and dates, summarise in groups, combine tables and reshape them. The last lesson uses all of it on one sales report whose totals look right and are not, and asks you to find out why.

hints: Count the grid cells without the labels.
Labels are not measurement cells.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each of the three shops has four monthly cells, giving 12.

questions.onCorrect: 12. Each of the three shops has a cell for each of the four months.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the shops and months. Each combination has its own cell.

hints: One output cell needs a single value.

questions.prompt: Which melt argument names the columns that stay attached to every measurement?
hints: Keep the identifier beside each resulting row.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: id_vars retains identifier columns while selected value columns are unpivoted.

questions.prompt: A four-row table melts three measurement columns. How many long-form rows result?
hints: Count one row for each melted cell.
Each original row supplies three measurements.
Multiply the rows by the melted columns.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each original row contributes three measurements, producing 4 × 3 = 12 rows.

questions.onCorrect: 12. Each of the four rows gives one long row for each of the three columns.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the counts. Each row gives a long row per column.

Add the two values.
Divide by how many values there are.
questions.onCorrect: 7. The mean of the two repeated records is their total shared equally.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the sum. The rule here is the mean.
